newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan enacts business as usual for China-ruled HK.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan enacts business as usual for China-ruled HK.

text.p: Acting 105 days before Hong Kong returns to China's rule, Taiwan's parliament on Tuesday adopted a law governing ties with the territory after it unites with the island's arch adversary.

The law, intended to ensure Hong Kong's role as a conduit for Taiwan's huge investments into China, calls for keeping ties unchanged with Hong Kong and with Macau after the Portuguese enclave reverts to Chinese sovereignty in 1999.
"I hope the Hong Kong-Macau Relations Act will maintain the friendly relations between Taiwan and Hong Kong and Taiwan and Macau," lawmaker Lin Chuo-shui said after the morning vote.

The law provides a legal framework for continued direct links with Hong Kong and Macau, focusing on their future positions as "special administrative regions" to skirt Taiwan's 48-year-old ban on direct contacts with communist China.
It also maintains Taiwan's trade, investment and cultural links with Hong Kong and Macau.

Taiwan's investments in Hong Kong are huge, but the colony is equally important as the main transfer point for an estimated US$30 billion in "indirect" investments Taiwan businesses have poured into China since a late-1980s political thaw.
Taiwan approved more than US$1.2 billion in indirect China investments in 1996, a 12 percent rise from 1995, and hundreds of millions more flow in through offshore subsidiaries.
Despite the new law's passage, Taiwan's future ties with Hong Kong remain uncertain as icy Taiwan-China relations have prevented Taipei and Beijing from negotiating on the matter.
China and Taiwan have been adversaries since the Nationalists fled to the island after losing their civil war to the Communists in 1949.
Some analysts expect Beijing will use Taiwan's reliance on Hong Kong to force political and economic concessions from it.
Taiwan is particularly vulnerable in trade.

Taiwan's exports to China grew to US$19.148 billion in 1996, mostly transshipped in Hong Kong, while imports from China were only US$3.06 billion. Taiwan exports to Hong Kong were US$26.805 billion, while imports were just US$1.705 billion. In both cases, Taiwan has far more to lose in a trade showdown.
Taiwan lawmaker Fu Kun-cheng said he hoped the law would facilitate talks on relations between Taiwan and the two territories after they are handed over.
"The Hong Kong-Macau Relations Act sets a good foundation for future negotiations on Taiwan-Hong Kong and Taiwan-Macau relations," Fu told the state-run Central News Agency.
Beijing says Taiwan's "reunification with the motherland" will stand out as China's only unfinished territorial task after the colonial era ends in Hong Kong and Macau.
China regularly proposes that the "one country, two systems" model pioneered by Hong Kong should serve as a model for Taiwan's return.
Under the model, Beijing has proposed to let Taiwan keep its capitalist system and even its armed forces in exchange for accepting the sovereignty of the communist People's Republic.

Lawmakers who oppose Taiwan's unification with China have pressed for a law that would not undermine the island's chances for eventual independence, while pro-unification deputies have pushed to keep Taiwan's mainland options open.
Taipei officially espouses reunification, but first wants to see political reforms on the mainland.
